episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, August twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.
<break time="1.0s"/>
The top story this week begins with MIT's final A.I. and education report, prepared by the Ad Hoc Committee on A.I. Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training, and continues in Feature Coverage from Innovating Higher Ed. Before proposing an A.I.-use policy, the committee asked what an MIT education is meant to help students learn, practice, demonstrate, and value. The report then presents eight principles, including humanity at the center, intentional teaching, context-specific choices, and augmentation rather than automation.

In the full Innovating Higher Ed analysis, Dr. Norma Jones examines why that principles-before-policy sequence may matter. A finished assignment may offer incomplete evidence of a student's reasoning when A.I. produces part of the work. Conversations about submitted work, process records, and portfolios may provide additional evidence when they match the learning goal. Preserving approved accommodations, assistive technologies, and accessibility remains part of that choice.

The analysis also considers mentored research. If tasks once handled by undergraduates are automated, an apprenticeship could narrow unless programs preserve meaningful student involvement or provide other guided practice. MIT's roadmap was written for MIT, and its relevance elsewhere depends on each college's mission, students, staffing, accessibility responsibilities, formats, and resources. Read the complete Feature Coverage for eight questions campus leaders can carry into local conversations about policy, assessment, and mentored learning, and open MIT's report via the links at innovating higher ed dot com.
<break time="1.0s"/>
In A.I. Workforce and Careers, two Los Angeles universities are opening different undergraduate paths into A.I.-era work. The Los Angeles Times reports that USC is starting the first cohort in its Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence, while UCLA is opening a freestanding Department of Digital Humanities and a new bachelor's degree.

USC's four-year program combines mathematical and statistical foundations, algorithm development, applications in areas such as robotics and agriculture, and required ethics coursework. The Times reports that USC expects about fifty new students each year and roughly two hundred students in the major at one time.

UCLA's program connects humanities study with technology and data-oriented work in fields including history, archaeology, sociology, race, and gender. Its earlier digital humanities program grew from a design capacity of about twenty-five students per year to more than two hundred students minoring in the field. The source package does not yet report graduate placement, earnings, retention, or learning outcomes for either program. UCLA's degree is digital humanities, not a standalone A.I. major.
<break time="1.0s"/>
For a practical back-to-school checklist, Clemson News is reminding students, faculty, and staff to protect restricted information, use institutionally approved services, verify generated material, disclose A.I. use when required, and remain responsible for final work.

Clemson's tools directory lists enterprise services reviewed against university privacy, security, and data-governance standards. A separate guide permits selected licensed tools for some categories of university information while keeping restricted data out of those systems. Other listed services are contingent on Clemson's CheckIT review, while public or unapproved services and third-party plug-ins are treated as separate risk categories.

For coursework, students are directed to follow the syllabus and instructor rules, avoid submitting unauthorized A.I.-generated work, and describe or cite their use when required. Instructors are asked to state permitted and prohibited uses explicitly. Clemson presents the reminder as campus guidance. It does not provide evidence that the guidance changes behavior or learning, and its approved tools and data classifications are local decisions rather than a model already shown to fit every institution.
<break time="1.0s"/>
Meanwhile at Florida State University, a thermodynamics course supplied a concrete example during national A.I. discussions at Google's New York headquarters. FSU News reports that assistant professor Ralm Ricarte built an A.I. study notebook from lecture notes, course materials, and problem sets for Introduction to Thermodynamics.

The university describes the notebook as restricted to user-uploaded sources and able to cite its responses. Students can use those course materials to create study guides, practice quizzes, and audio or video overviews. FSU's Academic Center for Excellence also offers workshops and drop-in hours where tutors help students organize class materials and build study resources with supported tools.

Associate Vice Provost Paul Marty represented FSU at the Google gatherings and at related leadership workshops with the Association of Public and Land-grant Universities. The university account documents a workflow and an institutional support structure. It does not report a participant count, comparison group, quantified achievement gain, or independent evaluation of the thermodynamics notebook.
<break time="1.0s"/>
At Penn State, a campus A.I. space is designed around visits that commonly last ten to thirty minutes. EDUCAUSE Review describes the A.I. Arcade as a low-stakes physical space where faculty, staff, and students can try premium tools, follow short guided activities, and play retro-inspired games with staff support.

Beginners can use structured pathways, while experienced visitors can move directly into experimentation. The arcade uses tablet stations, supports class visits and pop-up events, and encourages visitors to share artifacts and learn together. Accessibility professionals review the tools, and the team reports providing alternatives when a distinctive tool does not meet every access need.

Classroom examples include students creating music for a podcast series, turning parliamentary-procedure concepts into songs, recording one-minute podcast pilots, and returning to make cover art. Other visits have opened discussions about copyright and A.I.-generated outputs. The article offers a practitioner operating model built around access, a short task, nearby help, and reflection or collaboration. It reports no controlled comparison, participation total, validated learning measure, or independent assessment of the arcade's effects.
<break time="1.0s"/>
Finally, from the research front, a roughly twenty-three-minute lesson may have improved performance on the kinds of rational-thinking problems it taught without producing a reliable advantage on a separate test of scientific-argument judgment. Johanna Grimm and Tobias Richter report that pattern in two preregistered experiments published in Learning and Instruction.

The final analyses included one hundred forty-nine university students in the first experiment and one hundred fifty-five in the second. The computer-based lesson introduced analytic and intuitive thinking, several cognitive biases, practical reminders, and practice with immediate feedback. Against two different active comparison activities, the trained groups improved by about one point three to one point five correct answers on a sixteen-item rational-thinking measure.

The lesson did not produce a reliable advantage on a separate fifteen-item scientific-argument task. Both trained and comparison groups improved. In the second experiment, the comparison group showed the larger before-and-after gain, although the groups did not differ reliably at the posttest. The researchers suggest that repeating the argument test may itself have provided practice.

The study used immediate posttests at one German university and did not measure lasting effects, grades, classroom behavior, or real decisions. Next week, Innovating Higher Ed will examine the lesson itself, separate preregistered findings from exploratory results, explore how the test may have influenced performance, and outline measures for a cautious campus pilot.
<break time="1.0s"/>
That's this week's most applicable A.I. and innovation news for higher ed, covering the week ending August twenty-eighth, twenty twenty-six. Find full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com, and get Innovation Pulse by email or on X, YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and other major platforms.

leadStory.headline: Before Setting AI Guidelines, MIT Asked What Education Is For
leadStory.summary:
MIT’s final AI and education report asks what an MIT education should help students learn, practice, demonstrate, and value before turning to AI guidelines.

The report then considers where artificial intelligence could support that work and where it could perform work students need to practice.

In Innovating Higher Ed Feature Coverage, Dr. Norma Jones examines what that principles-before-policy sequence could mean for assessment, mentored learning, and campus policy.

The full analysis offers eight questions leaders can carry into local conversations and links directly to MIT’s report.
leadStory.broadcastFactBase:
MIT’s report presents eight principles, including humanity at the center, intentional teaching, context-specific choices, and augmentation rather than automation.

The report says unrestricted AI use can make some traditional assignments less reliable as evidence of individual learning. Conversations about submitted work, records of process, and portfolios may provide additional evidence when they match the learning goal. Preserving approved accommodations, assistive technologies, and accessibility remains part of that choice.

The report asks what may happen when tasks that undergraduates currently perform in mentored research are automated. An apprenticeship could narrow unless programs preserve meaningful student involvement or provide other guided practice.

The report is a roadmap for MIT, and its relevance elsewhere depends on each college’s mission, students, staffing, accessibility responsibilities, formats, and resources.
leadStory.source: MIT Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training / MIT

quickHits.headline: USC and UCLA Build Different Paths Into AI-Era Work
quickHits.summary:

The Los Angeles Times reports that USC is starting its first Bachelor of Science in Artificial Intelligence cohort while UCLA is opening a freestanding Department of Digital Humanities and a new bachelor's degree.

USC's four-year program is housed in the Mark and Mary Stevens School of Computing and Artificial Intelligence. It combines mathematical and statistical foundations, algorithm development, applications in fields such as robotics and agriculture, and required ethics coursework. The Times reports that USC expects about 50 new students per year and roughly 200 students in the major at one time.
